issues.subcategory: moral_incongruence operationalization contradiction
issues.description: The manuscript gives inconsistent definitions of the central construct. In the Abstract and hypotheses, moral incongruence is defined as the interaction of behavioral frequency and moral disapproval. In the Present Study section, it is instead defined as the interaction of moral disapproval with severity of consequences. This is not a minor wording issue because it changes the predictor and therefore the theoretical construct being tested.
issues.quote: Objectives: The present work seeks to clarify if moral incongruence (the interaction of behavioral frequency and moral disapproval of a behavior) ...; To accomplish this goal, we propose making use of an upcoming, nationally representative study ... Central to the proposed study is the measurement of moral incongruence as the interaction of moral disapproval of an action with severity of consequences from the action.

issues.subcategory: inconsistent sample-size descriptions
issues.description: The manuscript inconsistently describes the planned total sample size. The abstract says N=4,000 with n=2,500 representative and n=1,500 sports-wagering participants, which sums to 4,000 exactly, while the Methods says 'over 4,000' for the same components. This discrepancy is small but signals lack of precision in a registered report where exact sample plans should be fixed.
issues.quote: Methods: ... (N=4,000) involving a representative sample of the U.S. population (n=2,500) and a sample of sports-wagering individuals in the U.S. (n=1,500). ... This will provide us with a total sample of over 4,000 American adults.

issues.subcategory: nonrepresentative combined sample used for broad claims
issues.description: The study combines a matched general-population sample with a targeted oversample of sports wagerers, yet repeatedly frames the total as representative or nationally representative. Unless analyses properly account for the complex sample composition with weights or stratification, estimates and cross-domain associations may be distorted, especially for gambling-related analyses and any pooled analyses.
issues.quote: This work will make use of an upcoming study (N=4,000) involving a representative sample of the U.S. population (n=2,500) and a sample of sports-wagering individuals in the U.S. (n=1,500). ... To accomplish this goal, we propose making use of an upcoming, nationally representative study of addictions in the U.S. population

issues.subcategory: no weighting plan for YouGov sample
issues.description: No information is provided on whether survey weights will be supplied by YouGov or used in analysis, how the sports-betting oversample will be integrated, or whether population inferences will be weighted. For a matched panel sample plus oversample, omission of weighting/variance estimation procedures undermines evaluability and reproducibility.
issues.quote: Participants will be recruited by YouGov Opinion Polling and matched to U.S. representative norms. ... we will also recruit an additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports generally or sporting events specifically.

issues.subcategory: oversample likely induces collider/confounding in gambling analyses
issues.description: Recruiting an additional sample selected on past-year sports wagering strongly conditions on the target behavior for gambling analyses. If pooled with the general sample without a clear modeling strategy, the relationship between moral disapproval, frequency, and gambling problems may be altered by selection, making comparisons with other behaviors difficult and potentially biased.
issues.quote: we will also recruit an additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports generally or sporting events specifically.

issues.subcategory: modified ASSIST applied to unvalidated domains
issues.description: The ASSIST is being modified and extended to pornography and gambling, domains for which the authors acknowledge it is not validated. They then plan to use these modified items as outcome measures and, in some cases, as the basis for key comparisons across domains. This creates substantial construct-validity concerns because observed differences may reflect measurement artifacts rather than true domain differences.
issues.quote: We will also include pornography and gambling as response options on the NIDA-ASSIST... Although such an approach is not currently validated for gambling or pornography...

issues.subcategory: substantial alteration of validated ASSIST frequency item
issues.description: The authors materially alter the NIDA Quick Screen alcohol item from binge frequency (sex-specific 4+/5+ drinks) to any alcohol frequency. This changes the meaning of the measure from risky/heavy drinking to general use, weakening comparability with ASSIST scoring logic and potentially inflating associations with moral disapproval by conflating ordinary use with problematic use predictors.
issues.quote: Although we will include these response options, for the sake of the present study, we will look at alcohol frequency more generally (i.e., asking participants how often they have consumed alcohol without specifying the quantity consumed).

issues.subcategory: tobacco/nicotine measure contradiction
issues.description: The manuscript states that tobacco and non-cigarette nicotine products will be combined into a single question, but Table 1 lists separate outcomes for 'Tobacco/Nicotine products' while the text elsewhere refers to 'alcohol, tobacco, non-tobacco nicotine, prescription drugs, illicit drugs, cannabis' and later 'nicotine use'. It is unclear whether there is one nicotine variable or multiple, preventing clear understanding of the analytic set.
issues.quote: we will make it explicitly clear that smoked tobacco products, e-cigarettes/vapes, and smokeless tobacco products are all subsumed by our single question on tobacco/nicotine. ... Responses to each of the above five items will be averaged for each substance of interest (i.e., alcohol, tobacco, non-tobacco nicotine, prescription drugs, illicit drugs, cannabis).

issues.subcategory: frequency scale coding inconsistencies
issues.description: The coding of the same frequency scale is inconsistent across sections. The Methods text says pornography frequency is on a scale of 1 to 6, while the supplemental table shows 0 to 5. Similar inconsistencies appear for gambling. Such discrepancies matter because inclusion criteria are defined using these codes.
issues.quote: participants will report past-year frequency of pornography use on a scale of 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day). ... [Supplemental table:] Never (0) ... More than Once Per Day (5)

issues.subcategory: inconsistent gating rules for follow-up measures
issues.description: The manuscript states both that only past-year users will complete further problematic-use measures and that key measures will be administered to all participants regardless of engagement. These are mutually incompatible. This affects missing-data structure, sample sizes by analysis, and interpretation of zero values among nonusers.
issues.quote: Only participants who endorse past-year use will complete further measures of problematic use. ... For each target behavior and corresponding measure of problematic use or addiction, key measures will be administered to all participants regardless of their engagement in the behavior.

issues.subcategory: missingness assumptions contradictory and unrealistic
issues.description: The authors claim they anticipate no unplanned missingness, but also describe analyses on different subsets and a skip pattern excluding some participants from further items. This is planned missingness by design, not absence of missingness. The manuscript provides no strategy for handling item nonresponse, skip-related structural missingness, or how complete-case restrictions affect comparability across behaviors.
issues.quote: Additionally, we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data. ... Therefore, for each analysis, we anticipate having slightly different subsets of the total sample.

issues.subcategory: inappropriate averaging of heterogeneous ASSIST items
issues.description: The planned substance problem score averages five items with incompatible scale metrics and score ranges (three items 0-5; two items 0-3-6). The original ASSIST uses weighted sums, not simple means across such recoded items. Averaging these heterogeneous response formats yields a score with unclear meaning and unknown psychometric properties.
issues.quote: Participants will also respond to two questions ... on 3 point scale (0 = No, Never; 3 = Yes, but not in the past 3 months; and 6 = Yes, In the past 3 months). Responses to each of the above five items will be averaged for each substance of interest

issues.subcategory: outcome time windows are mismatched with predictor time windows
issues.description: The key predictor frequency is assessed over the past 12 months, while problem indicators are assessed over the past 3 months (ASSIST) and pornography problems over the last 6 months (BPS). This temporal mismatch weakens interpretation of interactions and comparability across domains, because predictors and outcomes do not refer to the same period.
issues.quote: participants will report the frequency with which they have engaged in those behaviors over the past 12 months ... To assess problematic ... use ... 'In the past three months...' ... Brief Pornography Screen ... 'In the last 6 months'

issues.subcategory: moral disapproval measured as single item for complex construct
issues.description: Moral disapproval is operationalized with a single item for each behavior. Given the study's central theoretical focus on moral incongruence, a one-item measure is a weak operationalization that may not capture intensity, salience, shame, conflict, or personal vs perceived social morality. This is especially problematic when interactions are tested, as unreliability attenuates interaction effects.
issues.quote: For each substance, we will ask participants to rate their agreement with the following statement “I believe that using ________ is morally wrong” on a scale of 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).

issues.subcategory: moral incongruence conflated with interaction term rather than discrepancy
issues.description: The paper treats the product of moral disapproval and behavior frequency as equivalent to moral incongruence. Conceptually, incongruence implies discrepancy between values and behavior, which may not be captured well by a multiplicative term on ordinal scales. A product term can be high for frequent users with modest disapproval and may not represent subjective conflict or distress directly.
issues.quote: moral incongruence is better conceptualized as the interaction of moral disapproval and use ... In this revised definition, use frequency moderates links between moral disapproval and self-reported feelings of addiction, and it is this moderation that represents moral incongruence.

issues.subcategory: behavior-frequency operationalization mismatch for gambling
issues.description: The methods first say gambling frequency will be assessed using a single item, but then say an average across gambling behaviors will be taken, and the supplement shows a single item 'Gambled or placed bets at all.' This leaves unclear whether gambling frequency is one global item or a composite across multiple gambling forms.
issues.quote: We will assess gambling frequency using a single item. ... To form a measure of gambling frequency, an average across gambling behaviors will be taken.

issues.subcategory: number of outcomes/analyses inconsistent
issues.description: The manuscript refers to 'eight proposed outcomes' and '8 moderation analyses,' but the listed target behaviors in some places total seven (pornography, gambling, alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, prescription drugs, illicit drugs), while other sections split tobacco and non-tobacco nicotine differently. The exact analytic family is unclear.
issues.quote: assumptions of regression ... will be tested for each of the eight proposed outcomes. ... In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses ... corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest

issues.subcategory: incorrect reporting of BPS response scale and scoring
issues.description: The BPS is described in the text as 0-2 scoring, but the supplemental measure displays 0-2-4 response coding. This affects summed totals and any standardized comparisons. Inconsistent scoring of a primary outcome is a serious preregistration problem.
issues.quote: Participants will respond ... on a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often). Responses are summed. ... [Supplement:] | Never (0) | Occasionally (2) | Very Often (4)

issues.subcategory: incorrect reporting of PGSI response coding
issues.description: The manuscript text states the PGSI uses a 0-3 scale, but the supplemental table codes categories 0, 2, 4, and 5. This is a direct scoring inconsistency for a main outcome and makes the planned averaging uninterpretable unless clarified.
issues.quote: This 9-item measure requires participants to respond ... on a 4-point scale of 0 (never) to 3 (almost always). Responses will be averaged. ... [Supplement:] | Never (0) | Sometimes (2) | Most of the time (4) | Almost Always (5)

issues.subcategory: using averaged PGSI instead of validated total without justification
issues.description: The PGSI is conventionally summed, with established cutoffs and interpretation. Averaging responses rather than using the validated total score changes the metric and may alter psychometric properties. No justification is given for deviating from standard scoring.
issues.quote: problem gambling behavior will be measured using the Problem Gambling Severity Index ... Responses will be averaged.

issues.subcategory: using both validated and unvalidated outcomes selectively across domains
issues.description: Pornography and gambling each have both domain-specific validated screens and modified ASSIST measures, whereas substances rely only on modified ASSIST averages. This asymmetry compromises cross-domain comparisons because any apparent uniqueness could derive from different outcome quality rather than substantive differences.
issues.quote: with pornography and gambling assessed using the validate measures of problematic use (the Brief Pornography Screen and the Problem Gambling Severity Index, respectively).

issues.subcategory: no explicit primary outcome selection among multiple outcomes
issues.description: For pornography and gambling there are two candidate outcomes each (validated scale and modified ASSIST), but the manuscript does not clearly designate which is primary for confirmatory tests and which is supplementary. This leaves room for selective emphasis depending on results.
issues.quote: Key dependent variables are listed in Table 1. ... Pornography Use | Brief Pornography Screen Sum Score and modified NIDA-ASSIST items; Gambling Behavior | Problem Gambling Severity Index and modified NIDA-ASSIST items

issues.subcategory: supplemental analyses left unspecified if assumptions violated
issues.description: The plan says that if OLS assumptions are 'substantially violated,' supplemental robustness analyses will be conducted 'as appropriate,' but gives no predefined decision rules or model alternatives. This invites post hoc analytic choice, especially with skewed zero-inflated outcomes where many alternative models are possible.
issues.quote: in cases where assumptions are substantially violated, we will conduct supplemental analyses to test the robustness of our models, as appropriate.

issues.subcategory: OLS modeling of bounded/ordinal/zero-inflated outcomes
issues.description: The outcomes are sums/averages of ordinal items with likely heavy floor effects and bounded ranges, especially for low-prevalence substances. Modeling them with ordinary least squares may be inappropriate; assumptions checks alone do not solve scale-distribution mismatch. Count, ordinal, hurdle, or zero-inflated models may be more suitable.
issues.quote: As a primary test of our key hypotheses, we will conduct moderation analyses using the lm function in the stats package for R statistical software

issues.subcategory: equivalence parameter specification unclear and inconsistent
issues.description: The equivalence procedure is under-specified and internally inconsistent. The manuscript states an SESOI of δ=.27, then later says the equivalence region is set to β=.11 and refers to hypotheses 2b/3b. It is unclear whether δ refers to standardized beta, raw coefficient, or another parameter, and the manuscript appears to contradict itself on the actual equivalence bound.
issues.quote: We will use the Anderson-Hauck equivalence test for regression ... with an equivalence region based on the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) of δ= .27. ... we elected to set our SESOI (δ) for our equivalence interval equal to the observed standardized estimate ... (β=.11 ...). ... setting our equivalence region to δ= |.11|

issues.subcategory: SESOI derived from incomparable prior effects
issues.description: The chosen SESOI is based on prior standardized estimates from different moderators (religiousness rather than moral disapproval), different outcomes, and different measures. Using these as the benchmark for equivalence in the present analyses is not well justified and risks an arbitrary null region.
issues.quote: Notably, this effect was observed for an interaction between religiousness (as opposed to moral disapproval directly) and pornography viewing frequency in predicting self-reported addiction. Additionally, this past work used a different and less rigorously validated outcome measure than those proposed for the current study

issues.subcategory: post hoc equivalence region based on observed pornography effect
issues.description: The plan explicitly proposes changing the equivalence region after seeing the data, using the lower bound of the observed pornography interaction confidence interval. This is data-dependent thresholding and undermines confirmatory inference, especially in a registered report intended to fix decision criteria ex ante.
issues.quote: we will conduct exploratory analyses wherein we redefine the region of equivalence using the lower bounds of the 95% CI for the standardized estimate for our pornography outcome. Specifically, we will use the lower limit of the 95% confidence interval around the obtained standardized estimate

issues.subcategory: power-contingent alteration of hypotheses/tests
issues.description: The manuscript states that if power is insufficient for some low-prevalence substances, analyses will be 'adjusted accordingly' by changing the equivalence region. This changes the inferential target depending on observed or projected sample sizes, reducing the confirmatory nature of the design.
issues.quote: Should we lack power to sufficient test equivalence with null effects for the above behaviors, we will adjust analyses accordingly. Specifically, rather than testing whether or not the effect ... falls within the region of equivalence for our primary SESOI, we will test an alternative model where our equivalence region is defined by the lower bound of the 95% CI ...

issues.subcategory: incorrect/ambiguous power analysis reporting
issues.description: The power analysis section contains incomplete and unclear phrasing ('a series of estimated achieved power based'), and Table 2 appears malformed. More importantly, power appears to be based on regression with one tested predictor and six predictors total, but does not address the use of interactions under subgroup restrictions, weighting, or equivalence testing specifically. Standard NHST power is not the same as power for equivalence tests.
issues.quote: we conducted a power analysis ... and a series of estimated achieved power based. The results are summarized in Table 2 below. ... All analyses conducted using G*power; assuming α = 0.05, regression models with 6 independent variables ... and 1 tested predictor.

issues.subcategory: malformed duplicated table footnotes
issues.description: Table 2 repeats the same footnote text multiple times and appears corrupted. This raises concern that the table may not accurately communicate the intended power assumptions or values.
issues.quote: 1. All substance estimates based on the 2019-2020 National Survey on Drug Use and Health ... | 1. All substance estimates based on the 2019-2020 National Survey on Drug Use and Health ... | 1. All substance estimates based on the 2019-2020 National Survey on Drug Use and Health ...

issues.subcategory: no handling plan for multiple testing across many analyses
issues.description: The study proposes multiple moderation analyses, direct-effect tests, equivalence tests, bivariate correlations, and potentially exploratory follow-ups, but no familywise error or false-discovery plan is given for the primary hypothesis tests. Holm adjustment is mentioned only for correlations, not the main analyses.
issues.quote: Bivariate correlations will be conducted across all included measures and reported using Holm-adjusted test statistics ... In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses

issues.subcategory: causal language from cross-sectional associations
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly uses causal or mechanistic language such as 'influences,' 'affects,' and 'predicts' in ways that imply explanatory precedence, despite a cross-sectional design with simultaneous self-reports. Such wording overstates what can be inferred and risks readers interpreting correlational moderation as causal moderation.
issues.quote: we seek to establish whether moral incongruence ... influences self-perceived feelings of addiction ... ; future research that fully accounts for the role of personal morality in affecting individual perceptions

issues.subcategory: claims about false-positive diagnoses unsupported by design
issues.description: The discussion suggests that findings would indicate false-positive diagnoses in clinical settings or bias in self-reported addiction research. The present study does not assess clinical diagnosis, clinician ratings, or objective behavioral dysregulation, so it cannot determine false positives or diagnostic misclassification.
issues.quote: it is likely that the effects of moral incongruence on feelings of addiction are most critical in treatment seeking populations. ... the real potential concern associated with this effect is whether it creates false-positive diagnoses in clinical settings.

issues.subcategory: hypothesis framing is confirmatory toward desired uniqueness conclusion
issues.description: The manuscript states an explicit goal 'of demonstrating' uniqueness of moral incongruence for sexual behavior. In a registered report, this phrasing suggests a directional advocacy orientation rather than neutral testing. It may also bias design choices toward proving uniqueness rather than fairly comparing domains.
issues.quote: with a specific goal of demonstrating that moral incongruence is unique in predicting compulsive sexual behaviors. ... Ultimately, we aim to demonstrate that ... the role moral incongruence in predicting feelings of dysregulation is unique to sexual behavior

issues.subcategory: overgeneralization from U.S. panel to addictions broadly
issues.description: The manuscript makes broad claims about 'the full spectrum of addictions' and recognized addictive disorders, yet the sample is U.S.-based, online-panel, and includes a sports-betting oversample. Cultural norms around morality vary substantially, as the authors partly note; conclusions about uniqueness across addictions are therefore context-limited.
issues.quote: demonstrating that other so-called addictive behaviors ... are well-predicted by moral disapproval ... and speculating that moral disapproval is likely present in the full spectrum of addictions, both substance and behavioral. ... a representative sample of the U.S. population

issues.subcategory: insufficient detail on YouGov quality-control and recruitment procedures
issues.description: The manuscript defers to YouGov's proprietary standards for data quality and therefore does not specify recruitment, exclusion, quotas, deduplication, or bot/inattention checks. Proprietary assurances are not enough for replication or appraisal of risk of bias.
issues.quote: certain measures of quality control and responsiveness are guaranteed as a part of their data collection process based on their proprietary data collection standards.

issues.subcategory: no preregistered participant exclusion criteria
issues.description: The authors state they do not anticipate removing responses for careless responding, but do not specify any exclusion criteria for speeders, duplicate responders, implausible patterns, or straightlining. Registered reports should define these contingencies in advance, especially in online panel research.
issues.quote: we do not anticipate having to remove responses from the dataset due to inattentive or invalid response styles or due to careless responding.

issues.subcategory: problem measures include guilt item, contaminating association with morality
issues.description: The BPS contains an item about continuing to use pornography despite feeling guilty. Because guilt is closely linked to moral disapproval, the pornography outcome partially embeds the predictor construct, inflating associations between moral disapproval and 'problematic use' and making cross-domain comparisons unfair, especially when other outcomes may not include equivalent moral-affective content.
issues.quote: 5. You continue to use pornography even though you feel guilty about it.

issues.subcategory: PGSI includes guilt item, contaminating gambling associations
issues.description: The PGSI includes a guilt item, which may similarly overlap with moral disapproval. This construct overlap means any direct effect of moral disapproval on gambling problems may partly reflect shared item content rather than distinct prediction of gambling disorder severity.
issues.quote: Have you felt guilty about the way you gamble or what happens when you gamble?

issues.subcategory: cross-domain outcome non-equivalence
issues.description: Pornography and gambling outcomes differ markedly in content from the ASSIST-derived substance outcomes; some include guilt and subjective problem recognition, others include urges, external concern, and functional impairment. Because the criterion constructs are not matched across domains, comparing interaction magnitudes to infer uniqueness is problematic.
issues.quote: Pornography Use | Brief Pornography Screen Sum Score and modified NIDA-ASSIST items; Gambling Behavior | Problem Gambling Severity Index and modified NIDA-ASSIST items; Alcohol | Average of modified NIDA-ASSIST items for specific substances

issues.subcategory: limited covariate set leaves major confounding unaddressed
issues.description: Only age, gender, and religiousness are included as covariates despite available panel variables including ideology, region, education, income, race, marital status, and religious affiliation. Since moral disapproval is likely correlated with many sociodemographics and political ideology, omitted variable bias could distort direct and interaction effects.
issues.quote: In each case, we intend on including religiousness, age, and gender as covariates ... [Supplemental materials list many additional panel variables]

issues.subcategory: gender coding noninclusive and analytically unclear
issues.description: Gender is modeled as binary in visualization despite mention of panel-provided gender and a coding of '1 = male, and 0 = not-male.' This collapses women and gender minorities together, is conceptually problematic, and may not match the sex-specific alcohol items in the survey logic.
issues.quote: gender (binary where 1 = male, and 0 =not-male)

issues.subcategory: sex/gender terminology mismatch in alcohol item logic
issues.description: The survey branching for heavy-drinking items uses 'IF GENDER = WOMAN' and 'IF GENDER = MAN,' but elsewhere the covariate is gender coded as male vs not-male. This mismatch between gender identity and sex-specific drinking thresholds is conceptually and operationally inconsistent.
issues.quote: IF GENDER = WOMAN ... more than 4 drinks ... IF GENDER = MAN ... more than 5 drinks ... gender (binary where 1 = male, and 0 =not-male)

issues.subcategory: unclear whether centering/standardization occurs in raw or standardized scales
issues.description: The plan says SPSS will be used to transform ASSIST items and religiousness into standardized variables, then says focal predictors and moderators will be entered in raw form during data processing and centered. It is unclear which variables are standardized before modeling and which coefficients are used for equivalence tests, affecting reproducibility and interpretation of beta thresholds.
issues.quote: SPSS will be used to transform the above-described ASSIST items and measures of religiousness into standardized variables. ... For moderation analyses, key variables will be entered in their raw form during data processing in SPSS, and their product will be computed.

issues.subcategory: no explicit code or formula for primary models
issues.description: The manuscript does not state the exact regression equations for each domain, whether outcomes are analyzed among users only or full sample, or how the two pornography/gambling outcomes will be handled. This lack of precision makes the registered analytic plan less reproducible than it should be.
issues.quote: As a primary test of our key hypotheses, we will conduct moderation analyses using the lm function in the stats package for R statistical software

issues.subcategory: low-prevalence subgroup analyses underpowered
issues.description: The authors acknowledge likely insufficient power for prescription drug misuse and illicit drug use, with estimated achieved power as low as .301 and .472. Nonetheless, they retain these analyses in the main plan. Such underpowered subgroup tests are unlikely to support meaningful equivalence conclusions and risk unstable estimates.
issues.quote: Prescription Drug Misuse | 3.5% | 140 | .057 | .301; Illicit Substances | 6%-12% | 240-480 | .032-.016 | .472-.764

issues.subcategory: structural missingness from user-only follow-up not addressed analytically
issues.description: If only endorsers complete problem items, nonusers will have structural missing data on outcomes. The manuscript neither clarifies whether zeros will be imputed for nonusers nor whether analyses will be restricted to users, each of which changes the estimand. This is particularly important because moral incongruence is theorized among users/disapprovers, not nonusers.
issues.quote: Only participants who endorse past-year use will complete further measures of problematic use.

issues.subcategory: direct effect of moral disapproval interpreted as evidence of incongruence
issues.description: Several hypotheses and discussion points treat a main effect of moral disapproval among users as meaningful support for moral incongruence. But if the revised theory defines incongruence as an interaction, the main effect reflects simple association and could arise from overlapping negative evaluations rather than value-behavior conflict. The manuscript does not clearly separate these concepts.
issues.quote: We do expect moral disapproval of substances among substance users to positively predict self-reported problems ... However, we do not expect to find that the interactions ... will contribute uniquely

issues.subcategory: comparison target mixes recognized and nonrecognized addictions inconsistently
issues.description: The rationale criticizes prior work for relying on behaviors not recognized as addictive, yet the present study still includes pornography, which is not itself a recognized addiction diagnosis, and uses self-reported addiction/problem scales rather than diagnostic assessment across all domains. This weakens the argument that the current study solves the prior conceptual problem.
issues.quote: this work did not evaluate established addictive disorders ... instead relying on self-reported feelings of addiction to behaviors that are either not recognized as addictive ... As such, the present work systematically explores these two critiques by extending them to recognized addictive behaviors

issues.subcategory: clinical implications exceed community-sample evidence
issues.description: The manuscript draws implications for diagnosis and clinical practice from a community/panel sample using self-report screening measures. Such findings may not translate to treatment-seeking or diagnostically assessed populations, especially given acknowledged differences in prevalence and symptom severity.
issues.quote: there would be additional evidence supporting the inclusion of moral distress as a diagnostic consideration in the ICD-11 for CSBD

issues.subcategory: registered report status lacks preregistration specifics
issues.description: Although labeled a Registered Report, the manuscript does not provide registration identifier, repository location, date, or a clear distinction between confirmatory and exploratory analyses beyond some narrative statements. This omission limits verification of preregistered commitments.
issues.quote: Moral Incongruence and Addiction: A Registered Report

issues.subcategory: correlation reporting phrase is nonsensical
issues.description: The phrase 'reported using Holm-adjusted test statistics' is statistically imprecise. Holm adjusts p-values or significance thresholds, not the test statistic itself. This suggests confusion in planned reporting.
issues.quote: Bivariate correlations will be conducted across all included measures and reported using Holm-adjusted test statistics

issues.subcategory: validated measures misspelled/grammatical error signals lack of care
issues.description: The manuscript says 'validate measures' instead of 'validated measures.' While minor, such errors in the central analysis description and other malformed text may reflect insufficient proofreading in a preregistered protocol.
issues.quote: with pornography and gambling assessed using the validate measures of problematic use

issues.subcategory: no reliability plan for single-item measures
issues.description: Internal consistency is proposed for included scales, but the study relies heavily on single-item moral disapproval and frequency measures, for which reliability cannot be assessed via alpha/omega. There is no discussion of their measurement error or any validation strategy.
issues.quote: Descriptive statistics for included measures, as well as measures of internal consistency for included scales (Cronbach’s alpha and Omega total), will be calculated
